B's own tests only check the stored value is not plaintext and differs from before, so they still pass despite the broken behavior. Neither change is wrong alone: B was correct when userUpdatePrisma stored raw values, and A is correct for PUT /api/user. Together they break the password-change flow.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds @updatedAt to Article.updatedAt, so every prisma.article.update (including any that only touches other fields) now bumps updatedAt automatically. Change B adds a views counter and calls prisma.article.update with { views: { increment: 1 } } on every article GET. Merged, each read of an article now bumps updatedAt, since the @updatedAt behavior applies to any update. Article lists are ordered by updatedAt desc (articlesListPrisma) and updatedAt is exposed in articleViewer, so merely viewing an article reorders the list and changes the reported updatedAt, even though the article content wasn't modified. Neither change causes this alone: before A, the view increment left updatedAt untouched; after A without B, only real edits bump it. This is a concrete wrong behavior arising only from the combination. The existing tests pass because none assert updatedAt stability across reads.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes solve the same problem (stale tags from deleted articles showing up in the tag list) in different ways: A deletes orphan tags from the database on article delete, B filters unused tags out at read time in getTags. Merged, the code does the cleanup twice and the two tests are literally identical. However, there is no behavioral breakage: the outputs agree (getTags returns only in-use tags either way), and A's deleteMany is harmless alongside B's filter. A concrete harm scenario is weak; the one risk is A's global deleteMany racing with a concurrent article creation that upserted a tag but hasn't yet connected it, which exists in A alone and is not newly caused by B. The overlap is redundancy rather than contradiction.

In the merged code the controller's filter is redundant because the DB already guarantees only followed authors' articles are returned, so the same work is done twice. The two filters are consistent (both derive from the follow relationship), so results are correct and tests pass; it is duplicate intent rather than a runtime failure. Both also make identical edits to articles.int.test.ts and add near-duplicate new tests.

A potential slug-uniqueness issue (two long titles sharing the same first 100 chars) exists, but that is introduced by A alone, not by the combination with B.

The new sort=created path orders by createdAt, which is not indexed, but that is only a performance gap, not incorrect behavior or duplicated work. The invalidation happens after next() completes, so the cache is dropped after the orphan tags are removed; a concurrent read between article delete and tag cleanup could cache a stale list, but the subsequent tag.deleteMany middleware call clears it again. No concrete wrong scenario arises from the combination.

Both fix the plain-text storage problem through different routes, which is overlapping in purpose, but B's endpoint is a new feature (change with current-password verification) and doesn't contradict A. The page-size semantics are inconsistent: a client walking pages from the default listing (10 per page) would see page=2 skip articles 11-20 if it equates page with the default size. Both tests still pass because each is correct in isolation (A's with no page param, B's with page param).

rows.explanation: Change A soft-deletes articles (sets deletedAt) and filters deleted articles out of article get/list/feed queries. Change B adds a tag-counts endpoint that counts articles per tag via prisma.tag's _count of the `article` relation, without filtering on deletedAt. After merging, a soft-deleted article remains in the database, so its tags still count it: create article 'One' with tag x, soft-delete it, and GET /api/tags/counts still reports x: 1 even though no visible article uses x (previously a hard delete removed the row and the count would drop). B's .filter(count > 0) was meant to hide unused tags, but soft-deleted articles keep tags alive in the counts. This is a runtime semantic mismatch where B's query relies on the assumption that deleted articles are gone, which A breaks.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes article slugs mutable on title change. Change B adds a RecentView table keyed by (username, slug) with no foreign key to Article, so the stored slug is only a string. Merged, when an article is renamed, existing RecentView rows keep the old slug. recentArticlesPrisma takes the latest 10 views, looks up articles by those slugs, and silently drops any view whose slug no longer exists (flatMap with ?? []). So a user who viewed an article and then had it renamed loses it from their recent list, and the dropped stale rows still consume slots in the take: 10 window, so fewer than 10 entries may be returned even though more valid views exist. Also, if the old slug is reused by a new article, the stale view would point to the wrong article. Neither change alone has this problem, because slugs were immutable before A, which is the assumption B's schema relies on. Related existing tests (e.g. Comment relations) are unaffected.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: In the merged code, articlesListPrisma orders by createdAt desc (A) but filters the cursor with updatedAt < cursor.updatedAt (B). The controller also uses the cursor article's updatedAt. Cursor pagination requires the filter field to match the sort field. If an article has been edited (updatedAt != createdAt), ?after=<slug> will skip or repeat articles. For example, if A (created Jan 1, edited Jan 10), B (Jan 2) and C (Jan 3) exist, the list is C, B, A; after=B yields before=B.updatedAt=Jan 2, so only articles with updatedAt < Jan 2 are returned and A (updatedAt Jan 10) is wrongly skipped. The reverse case can repeat items. B's own test sets updatedAt only (createdAt equals now, near-identical), so it likely still passes, hiding the mismatch.

After merging, PUT /api/user/image accepts any string, including "http://..." or "javascript:...", so the rule A introduced (images must be https or empty) is not enforced on this new path. Alice can send {image:"http://img.example.com/a.png"} to /api/user/image and get 200, whereas the same value to /api/user returns 400. Both tests pass independently, but the invariant A establishes is violated by B's new write path.
